input:
This example concerns a continuous stirred-tank reactor in which a neutralisation reaction is carried out, the reaction being first order in the limiting reactant, and the aim is to establish what conversion can be expected when the reactor is operating at steady state. The answer, on the usual idealised analysis, is a steady-state conversion of 85.2%.

By conversion we mean, as always, the fraction of the limiting reactant that is consumed in passing from the feed to the outlet stream. Since the reaction is first order, the local rate of reaction is directly proportional to the local concentration of the limiting reactant. The special feature of the continuous stirred-tank reactor is that vigorous stirring keeps the contents uniform, so that the composition everywhere inside the vessel is the composition of the outlet stream; the rate of reaction is therefore the same at every point in the vessel, and the steady-state material balance can be written in terms of that one rate, which greatly simplifies the analysis compared with a reactor in which the composition changes along the flow path.

The numerical data are as follows. The rate constant $k$ is 0.14 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time $\tau$ is 41 min. For the ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor, the conversion $X$ is related to these quantities through the expression $X = \frac{k \tau}{1 + k \tau}$, in which the product $k\tau$ appears as the governing group; that product evaluates to 5.74, and substitution into the expression duly gives the steady-state conversion of 85.2%.

Two assumptions underpin the whole calculation and should be stated plainly. The first is perfect mixing, which is what justifies treating the entire vessel as sitting at the outlet composition; any departure from it means that the simple balance no longer holds exactly. The second is constant density, which allows the mean residence time to be identified with the ratio of the vessel volume to the volumetric throughput. It is worth stressing that these assumptions remain unchecked for the vessel in question, inasmuch as tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, so phenomena such as bypassing or the presence of stagnant zones would pass unnoticed, and any of them would tend to reduce the conversion achieved in practice.
target:
A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The steady-state conversion is 85.2%.

Conversion is the fraction of the limiting reactant consumed between the feed and the outlet. For a first-order reaction, the rate at any point is proportional to the concentration of the limiting reactant at that point. In a continuous stirred-tank reactor the vessel contents are uniform and sit at the outlet composition, so the rate is the same everywhere in the vessel, and the steady-state balance on the limiting reactant closes on that single rate rather than on a rate that varies along a flow path.

The rate constant $k$ is 0.14 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time $\tau$ is 41 min. For an ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor, the conversion $X$ follows from the product of the rate constant and the residence time: $X = \frac{k \tau}{1 + k \tau}$. The product $k\tau$ is 5.74, and substitution gives the steady-state conversion, 85.2%. The figure is a steady-state figure: during start-up the outlet composition is still moving towards its steady value, and the conversion passes through lower values on the way there.

The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density. Perfect mixing is the assumption that places the whole vessel at the outlet composition; where mixing falls short, part of the vessel sits nearer the feed composition, the local rate there is higher, and the single-rate balance no longer describes the vessel. Constant density is the assumption that makes the mean residence time the ratio of the vessel volume to the volumetric feed rate. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual vessel: tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, so bypassing or stagnant zones, if present, would go undetected, and either would lower the conversion of the installed reactor below the ideal figure.
